title: Awakening, Cessation, and Vulnerability, with Stephen Snyder

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, Vajrayana, tantra, Zen, predictive processing, psychedelics, non-duality, consciousness hacking, and much, much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Stephen Snyder. Stephen Mugen Snyder Sensei began practicing daily meditation in 1976. Since then, he's studied Buddhism extensively, investigating and engaging in Zen, Tibetan, Theravada, and Western non-dual traditions. He was authorized to teach in the Theravada Buddhist tradition in 2007 and the Zen Buddhist schools of Soto and Rinzai in 2022. Stephen is a senior student of Roshi Mark Sando Minnenberg, and a transmitted teacher in the White Plum Asanga, the body of teachers in the Maezumi Roshi lineage. Stephen is the author of many books, including Trust and Awakening, Demystifying Awakening, and Buddha's Heart. And now, without further ado, I give you a conversation with Stephen Snyder.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Stephen, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Thank you, Michael. It's a pleasure to be here with you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a pleasure to have you here. You know, something I don't think I've ever mentioned to you is that I first heard about you when I was at the Forest Refuge, and I was doing a self-guided three-month retreat there. This was a long time ago, and as part of it, I did allow myself to read Dharma materials a few hours a day, a small amount, but one of the main things that was there at that time was material from you and also Tina Rasmussen. And so I was aware of this person, Stephen Snyder, who was talking to me about meditation every once in a while during my long, long, long retreat decades ago, essentially, or at least 15 years ago, something like that. So it's very interesting and some kind of closing of the circle for me to have you on the podcast. So I'm so glad you're here.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, me too.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, do you want to say anything interesting about that material I was reading at the time that was mainly Pa Auk-influenced meditation stuff?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, I still lead jhana retreats at least once a year. I'm doing one in April for two weeks. I think there's something that's terribly important about those practices. In my teaching, I call this breath awareness meditation. So it's being aware of the breath in a specific location, which is between the nostrils and the upper lip and prioritizing that object above all else in experience or perception. And so it really helps us hone our ability as concentration meditators, as well as we're learning to turn away from our stories, our thoughts, our sense of self in a way that's extremely beneficial.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: The deeper experiences of that practice, it's called absorption or jhana. And to me, it's a slight slice of a particular quality of the absolute, which is what I call the source. And so we're experiencing these different qualities. And in the Pa Auk lineage, as you mentioned, who I studied with and was authorized to teach, the experience of jhana would be one where there would be no sense of self, so no self-referencing available, nor would there be any thought. So the experience is one of really awareness and consciousness merging with the meditative object in a kind of unity experience, but with full awareness, full consciousness. So there's full perception, but no concept. We can't conceptualize, we can't compare and contrast the experience. So it allows us this really deep experience. And one of the interesting features of this practice is the jhana itself feels like a radio frequency of energy. It's like there's a certain resonance of energy in each jhana. And part of the reason we do this practice, and this practice predates writing even. This was done as an oral tradition, a yogic tradition, and then, of course, in Hinduism and now Buddhism. And part of it is a purification of mind, the harmonization, the recognition of that, say, frequency for our consciousness to develop to match that frequency. Then we are done with that level of purification of mind. So it's a great precursor to making contact. And in the old ways, in the Theravadan practices, one can go from what's called the eighth jhana. There are eight jhanas. One can go from the eighth jhana directly into the absolute. But in my teaching, I call it the ninth jhana. So this can not only purify the mind, develop concentration, but we can open and access the source. And again, it's not 100% of people, but it is a possibility, there is a portal there for that practice.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And for you, was that in your own journey, your first connection with the source, or were you already fairly advanced in your practice?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: When I did that retreat, I had been practicing something like 20 or 25 years as a Zen student, predominantly, some Tibetan practice as well. But I'd done a lot of retreats. I probably did about four retreats a year for most of my 50 years I've been meditating. And I'd had several recognized Kensho or Zen awakenings prior to that. So I think I came in with a softer sense of me than the average person. So when it came time to put down the sense of self and thought, it wasn't a terribly uncomfortable prospect. I knew that and appreciated that experience.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And just to be clear, if I'm not mistaken, in the sort of spectrum of possible depths of jhana, everything from incredibly ultralight jhanas that partake of some of the jhana factors to the absolutely deepest illuminated absorption type jhanas, you're talking about, with Pa Auk, the far right end, right? The absolute deepest jhanas possible.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Right. As far as I know, we have the highest bar to confirm something as jhana. And I think from what I know, among the Western teachers that teach the Pa Auk system, I'm probably the most strict in that regard, too. I really want people to have that deep experience that's unmistakable. And so for me, even a short experience, I wouldn't confirm. I'd want to see somebody have a more sustained experience to really have it land in consciousness. But that is true. We're considered the most strict or have the highest bar, however you want to language it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And what would you consider to be long enough to really have a taste of that very deep level of jhana?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Most of my teaching, and I teach not only the jhanas, but also the heart practices, the Brahma Viharas, and also different awakening practices, I really find that unless somebody has at least a minimum of a 30-minute uninterrupted experience in these different areas, it isn't significantly life-changing. For most people, that 30-minute mark, something shifts that doesn't shift back exactly. So rather than if somebody has, say, a five-minute experience, it's important, it's good to validate it and to confirm for them, okay, you've experienced it, this is accessible to you, nothing bad happened. And then that will give them more of the confidence to open up to and abide longer in that next experience. With the Zen awakening, Kensho, and the cessation experience of Theravada, it seems to be that's an important threshold.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, some people have said that the ability to do these deep jhanas is actually not available for some percentage of people, almost like characterologically. Have you noticed anything like that?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: On most of these retreats, probably the maximum number that would have contact with jhana would probably be 50% or less. And that would be any contact. But what I will say is on the retreats I've taught, and I've taught this for 20 years now, everybody will get deep into the second level of concentration meditation called access concentration. And on the high end of that, we have these wonderful jhana factors of piti joy, sukha bliss, one-pointedness and equanimity and such that really make it so pleasurable and comfortable. We can meditate for long periods of time. We're not plagued by a lot of our normal obsessive thinking. We're not worrying too much. We're not in any kind of fear around annihilation, as you mentioned earlier. So it gives us more confidence. And there is a purification of mind that does happen with access concentration. And it's sometimes called something like the doorway to jhana or something like this. There's some languaging in the old material that talks about that it still is important. It's not the same because there still is thought and a sense of self, but it's pretty refined.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thank you for discussing the deeper end of jhana. It's really, really interesting. And in fact, we could probably do a whole show on it. But I want to switch mildly here to your new book, which is called Liberating the Self, Transforming Dysfunction into Authenticity, and see if we can unpack some of the really interesting material here. Anything you want to say overall about this text?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, this is, I think, a really interesting book. How this evolved was just in my own journey. I've done extensive retreat practice for, as I say, about 50 years now. And part of what I realized probably about 15 or 20 years ago was that other than working with therapists, trying to work through the different psychological issues that I had, I found that my meditation career wasn't adequately addressing, I'd say, my dysfunctional humanity. And so even though I had access to transcendent states and I could, was sort of contact ongoing, there still were times when I was having outbursts and anger and upset driving and frustrated with my partner and all these different things. And so I could tell that even though I was in touch with this really deep place, it wasn't making its way sufficiently into my personality material. And so I began working with the Diamond Approach, which I did for about 15 years, including the eight-year teacher training they have, the seminary. I didn't become a Diamond Heart teacher, but I really got to appreciate the relationship between the personal work and the spiritual work. I call it transformational and transcendent. And so that really helped me a lot work through my issues.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: I don't teach the Diamond Approach, but what I found working with students, and I do a lot of one-on-one work. I normally do between five and eight one-on-one sessions, Monday through Friday. So I work with students a lot. And what I found was when they were working with an emotion that was challenging, say somebody had a repetitive emotion of anger, getting them to recall the last experience of anger, and then helping them meditatively move to the vulnerability preceding the anger reaction, that was where I found there was a lot of potential to work. And if they could abide in that vulnerability, which normally for anger is some form of weakness, and physically we can feel it like ice water in our arms and legs, I can barely lift my arm, I feel weak, that kind of experience. But I found if they could stay with that and abide with the vulnerability, the vulnerability turned into the portal and that would open up to the quality of the absolute, which was authentic strength. And that's actually what we were hoping to draw upon for the incident at hand. And I found with working with individuals, and I've tried it with a few groups, that this wasn't 100% change from one experience. But it began opening this portal. And they began to realize, oh, the vulnerability is important to abide with, not just to jump over it and get to anger or hatred or whatever the strong emotion is. But to stay with that vulnerability was really the key. And that's really what I've seen folks doing. So I began sort of keeping track of what I was working with, what I was noticing in my own meditation. And then I do teach the heart practices we call the Brahma Viharas. And same thing, I was seeing the psychological places people were getting snagged. And if I could help them meditatively come to the vulnerability preceding the reaction, then that ended up becoming, again, the portal. And so that ended up leading to this book. And I included the Theravadan concentration or Samatha practices because they function in a way of helping us gradually deconstruct the self by identifying the concepts of me in all these different ways. So long answer to a short question.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, no, extremely interesting. So, can you unpack just briefly how we're using Theravada practice to notice these aspects of the sense of self or notice these ideas of me?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Sure. Well, one of the practices we have is called 32 Body Parts. And it's body parts like skin, hair, all the organs, so things like brain, heart, all these different parts of the body. And we meditatively get in contact with these. And the way I teach it is we want to make contact, but then we want to stay with it. So we drop beneath the conceptual contact with it. And we know we're in the conceptual contact when we're getting all the ideas about it. If I'm working with skin, for example, oh, you know, I don't like the shade of my skin. I get sunburned too easy. I remember when I got sunburned when I was five and it was really painful. Oh, when I was five, I had a wonderful birthday party. So if it's kicking up a lot of memories and concepts and relationships, that's still a conceptual contact. When we drop down to the non-conceptual, say with skin, we're going to have this deep felt sense of skin without actually knowing what it is. There'll be a kind of mystery about it.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: And when we can get to that level and have that sustained contact long enough, it seems that it loosens the concept of me as skin. And it's one way that deconstructs the me. As you know well, Michael, part of our sense of self is really identified with the body. And that's what we're learning in that practice. And there's other practices like the four elements, earth, water, fire, and air. And using those, the same thing, we go in and locate, we call characteristics of each of these. Like earth element would have hardness and softness as the first two characteristics. And so we find hardness in our body, bones, teeth, and we meditatively get to the non-conceptual contact. And the same thing, it seems to just let go of one piece of me. And as we keep going, it ends up just lightening and lightening that connection, which makes us more open to the transcendent because we're not worried about the abandonment of the body, which equals into the death of the body in terms of our conceptual fear.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Very, very interesting. So where would you then go from there?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, then I would normally introduce people into the awakening practices. And there's two paths that I teach for that. The Theravadan path, the cornerstone of Theravadan awakening, the four stages of awakening, requires an experience of cessation. And cessation is the ceasing of all materiality and mentality. So it's a lights-out, blackout experience. And the closest we have is like a dreamless sleep, where you fall asleep, it's just black, and you wake up. There's nothing, no content at all. But it's very particular in that if one has the experience of cessation, and again, if it's 30 minutes or more, then there's going to be a quality that I'm calling awakeness. And the book I'm writing now has to do with awakeness. I'm looking at awakeness in all these different practice areas, the jhanas, the heart practices, and the awakening practices. So that's part of what I look for in confirming somebody's awakening is the awakeness quality, how bright, how open, how shiny. There's all these ways that people will present. And then the other path I offer is the Zen path. So there's two paths there, which can be separate or intertwined. The one is Shikantaza, which translates as just sitting.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: But the way I teach it, I have three steps in it. And the last step is opening to the vastness. So opening to the space quality of the absolute, the source. And basically, we're abiding in the source directly. And that really both builds a comfort and confidence, but it also lets us relax more and more and more to realize I don't need to manage much of my life. There's this source that's doing all this. So it really lets us relax quite deeply. And that can lead in itself to an awakening experience. And the other path that I teach is the formal koan study, which is working with spiritual paradoxes that are systematized. We have about 600 or 700 koans in our lineage, and one would work through all these koans, which with each koan, there would be a mini awakening at least, which helps flesh out and knock off the stalactites and stalagmites of the cave of awakening, as it were.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So fascinating. In an earlier part of the day today, you and I were talking about this with you asking me questions about this topic, but I want to come back to you and see how you conceptualize this and how you work with this for yourself and with students. And that is what we were talking about earlier, like the psychological dimension and how much working with challenging emotions, working with really difficult life situations. You said you use vulnerability as the portal. But to what extent is this kind of psychological work important in your view? And how do you have people really engage that? And furthermore, I'm just going to keep unpacking the question, how do we balance it with the concentration and depth and cessation and spaciousness parts of meditation?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: That's, as you know, a big question. I think it's terribly important. As I said some years ago, I was very clear and my teachers were clear that I had had several deep Zen awakenings that teachers confirmed, but I still could see that my behavior didn't always match. In fact, my outside didn't always match my inside. And that's what I see with people is that we can have deep experience. And as you well know, it's easy for us as humans to then take the awakening or realization as a personal possession. Okay, I, Stephen, am now cool because I've had this awakening, so I'm cool, Stephen. That creates a whole new identity, or maybe it's a half step from our other identity, but it creates a whole new issue we have to work with and another self we have to investigate and hopefully deconstruct. So I think it's terribly important. I think the application of therapy is terribly important when it's appropriate. Some people, it's obvious that there have been life issues that are not resolved. And for example, I might see somebody who's working a death of a parent or a divorce, for example, where every time they talk about it, they break into tears. And it's been years since it happened. Or there's a way that they're still snagged by that event. So that's one of the things I look for is a repetitive, undigested piece of material. And I'm not a therapist, so I do recommend people get therapeutic help for that. But in the same token, I also look at it that we're on a spiritual path. So it isn't just becoming a super shiny ego that's also not our goal. But getting a good enough established vessel to hold the absolute and let the absolute have the fullest expression possible is helped a lot by doing personal work.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: And what I find is like doing exercises and the practices that I have in Liberating the Self. Oh, and by the way, I did change the subtitle. It's now Buddhist Practices for an Authentic Life. But I found that with folks doing this, it begins to soften those emotions. And also, when they have a strong emotional reaction, they know now, well, can I feel, can I sense into the vulnerability preceding this? Can I abide with that? And so that softens the sting of the vulnerability. Most of us, when we hit a vulnerability, we run as fast as possible or return to one of our escapes to not have to deal with it. So this is learning how to put our feet back in the fire in a healthy way. So I do see it having very positive effects. And in the next book on awakeness, I'm also identifying qualities of awakeness and I'm developing practices to cultivate those. And that seems to be when those are cultivated, when one works with the vulnerabilities in Liberating the Self, and then in the next book I have, I think that'll create a more complete package of working with vulnerability, opening to the absolute, and then entering the absolute through the positive qualities of awakeness, I think synthesizes into a kind of personal, individual expression of the absolute. The absolute is us, and we begin to function more cleanly as the absolute doing these specific practices.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: This is super interesting. When I look into the book, I see that you actually go into specific challenging emotions. And the sense I get of this is that you're coming from a Buddhist view that difficult emotions are sort of the unenlightened versions of enlightened emotions. They're like distortions of what's really there.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Exactly. Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And I'm curious if you would just take one particular specific challenging emotion and talk us through how we might work with that, reveal its authentic enlightened quality.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Okay. Well, I started with the example of working with anger and obviously is a common emotion reaction. So part of my teaching with students is I have them maintain a spiritual journal. My hope is that maybe at the end of each day, they can write down how their day went, specifically around places where they felt incongruent, where they overreacted or they reacted in a way that they said, you know, who was that? What was that? And so that starts creating a bit of a pattern. It starts painting a picture.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: But virtually everybody has anger to work with. So like if we were working now, you and I, I would say to you, okay, Michael, remember or recall the most recent time that you got really angry and not just, you know, slightly perturbed when you were really in the throes of anger. And so I'd have you relay that memory to me. Okay, I was driving, this person cut me off, we almost crashed and I yelled out the window at him and was really upset. Okay. So feel that upsetness, feel that anger now. Okay. How do you feel it? Well, I'm feeling this churning in my body. Energy is just going really quickly and I'm clenching my hands and feeling my muscles and all this. So I'm feeling like I want to take some action. I want the other person to know they did something wrong. Okay. So where in your body are you feeling anger specifically? Okay. Well, I can feel it in my hands. I can feel in my chest, the tightness in my chest, my legs and feet are poised to start running towards somebody. So I can feel all this energy in the body. Okay. So feel that. So find the somatic source as well. Okay. Now let's start to unpack the first experience. You were driving and somebody cut you off. Try to get to the front before the anger reaction. What was it like when they began cutting in? What was the moment of vulnerability there? And if they can move into that territory, which over time most people can, they would say, yeah, I'm starting to feel this sort of churning in my gut. I'm feeling a little coldness in my chest. I'm feeling a little weak in my arms and legs.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Okay, can you be with that right now? Yeah, yeah, that's fine to be with. Okay, so just be with that sense of weakness. We can call it weakness. Be with the vulnerability. Really let yourself land in this. You're totally safe, but let yourself really feel this vulnerability. And so they begin to feel it and feel like, yeah, I was really scared. I thought for a moment I might die. So it really triggered a fear reaction in me, a really strong fear reaction. Okay, so are you feeling anything different in your body? Yeah, my heart. I feel my heart is beating, but I'm feeling a tenderness in my heart. Okay, let's include that too. So let's just stay with that vulnerability and that fear, the fear you were going to die. And by just staying with it sort of through language and through meditation, it begins to open to where they'll start saying, you know, I'm feeling more stable. Like I'm feeling my feet on the ground. I'm feeling a strength returning to my arms and legs. And I'm feeling this confidence, this clarity. My mind is clear. It's not fuzzy. The fear isn't here. I feel a real directness. And so they start getting in touch with the quality of strength of the absolute. And they can tell because it's not personal. It's not I'm making this strength or I'm going to strength. They're feeling it naturally arising in their body, feeling the strength in their arms and legs, feeling the determination, say, in their chest or head.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: And again, I'm doing this very quickly. This might take 30 or 60 minutes to work through. I'm going to do the first retreat of this practice is in May, where we'll do more seminar meditation. People will work in small groups and individually in big group, and we'll work these issues. Part of it is also them exploring their history. You know, what's your history with anger? Well, it wasn't acceptable in my family, or my family was really angry. And you start getting, what's the norm you grew up with around this? What's your familial and your social and cultural attitudes towards anger, let's say? So all this helps us begin to unpack it. It's not like it goes away with one piece of work, but it starts that channel of opening to the absolute and seeing that the vulnerability isn't an ugly word. It's actually an important practice portal for us to take.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Super interesting, Stephen. What's the growth path here with this kind of work? Is it a long, slow chipping away at these various difficult emotions? And furthermore, in your teaching, what's your overall view of challenging emotion? Is it the case that we want to end up in a kind of place where we never have any difficult emotions, or is it more that we begin to recognize them as awake energy early on in their manifestation, and we allow this full display of the whole palette of emotion because we're able to ride it?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Well, I see the answer is both. That there's some benefit that we get just personally, but also we have to recognize we're humans and the potential for awakening is endless. The potential for penetrating the depths of the absolute, we can't ever find an end to it. So it's always ongoing. I would expect, and what I'm observing in students who have been working with me for a while is the reactivity is lessening. It still may happen, but it's getting to more core issues. You're kind of resolving the lighter stuff and going to more deep issues and resolving those. So it's not like major triggers are happening by and large. People will get triggered, say, with anger, but it'll be something that's fairly fleeting. And what happens sometimes is they can be with the vulnerability, feel the anger starting and the portal opens to the absolute. So they find both there's a psychological anger reaction and there's also the flow of the absolute with strength. I can be here. I don't need to be angry with you. I can be present, but I can be clear and firm. Stop. That's it. You're done. That strength can come across even if there is some psychological reaction.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes, it's very, very interesting. You also include in this book something that you call protective meditations. How would you define that, and what is the purpose?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, the protective meditations are part of the traditional Theravadan practice path, the Samatha practice path. And one of them is fairly obvious, which is unconditioned love, what I call unborn love or metta. And then there's also recollection of the Buddha. And I actually have done daylongs on recollection of the Buddha, where part of my teaching we haven't touched on is I do some guided meditations into the absolute. And for whatever reason, probably 95% of the people on a retreat can follow along with what I'm describing unfolding in our field. And so they can end up coming along with me into the absolute and making their own direct contact. So recollection of the Buddha, I do the same thing. I do a guided meditation where we end up going to where the Buddha is teaching. And people will have the experience of sitting in the audience, having the Buddha teach. And so for Buddhists, this is quite impactful. And one thing I do when I do this is I never describe the Buddha. And so afterwards, I'll ask people who say, yeah, I saw the Buddha. I'll say, how did he appear? What did he look like? How old was he? And interestingly, people will often have the same, they'll see him in the same age group and he'll appear in the same, for example, luminosity or what have you. So it's quite interesting that people can have that connection.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Another one of it is the foulness meditation where in the old days we'd go to what they called the charnel grounds where they cremated the dead bodies. And the Buddhists would meditate in these charnel grounds with these partially cremated bodies.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: This is the one where we have a list of various types of dead bodies to see, like someone who has drowned and someone who's chopped up.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Exactly, that's it. And modern-day practitioners, not many, but a few will do things like they'll find a way to attend an autopsy, for example, and they'll use that as their charnel ground meditation. And then the final meditation is recollection of death, and this is our own death. So that's a really interesting practice. When I did all these with my teacher, these were all brand new to me. I'd never heard of the practices. And I had a certain amount of skepticism when I was presented with them of like, you know, you're going to just practice meditating on your own death. And I'm like, okay, you know, we'll see what happens. And lo and behold, you're meditating and all of a sudden you're seeing yourself. And the irony here is everybody I know has done this practice always sees themselves as really, really old. Nobody saw themselves like in a car accident six months from now. It was always, oh, yeah, I think I'm like 90.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: But you get to see, you know, the dying and sort of the quality of life, the quality of spirit at that time. And we can see that there's a trajectory here. If I continue on this path, look at how much easier this death is going to be than I anticipate. Look at how smooth it is. And then also, what can I do now that's going to make that a better experience? So these all help us protect us for going into the absolute and opening to cessation. So it's sort of giving us protection and also loosening our connection to the body in this lifetime. And so to me, that's the strategy of it, of why we do those.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good. And so this leads us to the culmination here, which is what you're calling silent illumination meditation. And I know there'll be a lot of interest in hearing more detail on this. So tell us about Shikantaza, the way you teach it.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah, Shikantaza, when I learned this as a young Zen student, the instructions were elaborate on the physicality, meaning your posture, I mean, how our robes were, all these different things, how we sat on our cushion were very strongly emphasized. No information or content was given about the internal experience. So shortly after doing my first retreat, I went around to the folks who were the most experienced there. And of course, in those days, maybe 10 years was the most senior person. And I asked them, what are you doing in Shikantaza? And the people that gave me an answer, I got every answer you can imagine what they were doing. And what I concluded was nobody knew at all what to do in the meditation. They were all doing it, but it was going in all these different directions.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: And so when I began sort of actively teaching Shikantaza a few years back, I began to see the tie-in between the Theravada and jhana practice and the Zen practice, that actually there was a morphing that happened when it came from India to China and incorporated into Taoism and Confucianism. There really was a shift in the jhana practice, and part of it was because in jhana practice, people have a lot of expectations. You have to manage people's expectations and disappointment and striving. The teachers began not giving a lot of the instructions and letting people have the experience so they weren't striving for a particular state. But what happened was they ended up removing so much of the material that then it just was this open sitting. People are sitting and hoping something happens. So knowing that, I sort of deconstructed the jhana practice into three stages. The third stage, we're going sort of highest, lowest. The third stage would be entering into the vastness, opening into the absolute.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: And what precedes that in the third stage is the dissolving of the body boundary, the sense of me being contained in the skin. And to me, this is one of the most primary identifications we have. We're infants when we establish hunger's inside this thing, food is outside this thing. So we get I'm hungry. I'm here. So that's the third stage is the softening of the body boundary and opening to the vastness. The second stage is unity of inner and outer. And the first stage is unity of body mind. So normally with this practice, I would take people start the meditating and then say, okay, now bring your awareness to your interiority. And just notice is your body and mind in a unity, in a oneness, or is there a separation? And for most people who have a separation, it's usually somewhere around the neck. There's a concept of I'm here in the head and this is my body from the neck down. And so we just hold that head, body, mind, body, and separation. And meditatively over a period of time, that concept will soften. The concept of separation softens and people will feel a flow, a unity of body-mind. That's stage one.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Then they take that as their interiority, but make contact with the exterior and do the inside and outside match, or are they different? And as we're holding both of these and particularly becoming aware of the body boundary, then the body boundary begins to soften. It gets to where I can't feel my left arm, my head is gone, or my leg feels like it's two meters, six feet in that direction. And so enough of the body boundary is gone, then I just have folks open awareness to the vastness, to the absolute, and there's just an abiding in the absolute. So that becomes the bulk of the meditation, which really helps soften that fear and concern about what's going to happen. And then I'll throw in one last line, and I'm sure you know this from your teaching, Michael, that one of the issues that's recurrent on a spiritual path is aloneness. And we meet it at different levels, sort of on a personal level than we can meet it when we're accessing the absolute as well. And we have to work with that aloneness because that's part of what drives our personality to either connect or to have some type of arrangement that we don't feel isolated or alone. So anyway, those are the three stages I have for Shikantaza, which is not in the usual Zen presentation. That's something I've introduced to my teaching.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And I imagine that you find this to be much more helpful, students find this to be much more helpful than the throw them in the deep end and hope they figure it out version.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: Yeah. And that's how we learn, but it works for some people, a small percentage, but a lot of people, it doesn't work. transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Excellent. Now, again, I'm not sure exactly how you're using vocabulary, so I'll just ask the question the way I'm talking about it. Now, when people are resting in the absolute, do they then find that they're having cessation experiences?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: It's a little more involved than that. Abiding in the absolute, I don't consider that to be an awakening. I'll just mention awakening, then we can talk about cessation. For me, there has to be three components for an awakening. There has to be a deep sense of absence of self or no self. And there has to be a deep connection to the unity, the oneness of the absolute as well, which is the love component. So there's the emptiness, the love presence. And then there has to be a third component, the recognition, this is who I truly am. And you can have any of those independently, which are helpful experiences, but I have to see all three for me to confirm a Kensho experience, an awakening experience. And there can be different depths. I talk about this in my book, Demystifying Awakening. There's three levels in the Zen tradition.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder
transcript.text: So shifting to the Theravadan model, like on the guided meditations I do on retreat, one of the ones I do each day is I do it deep into the absolute, but specifically focusing on the darkness, the absence, emptiness, the peace and stillness. And the way I teach in my experience is that cessation is the source of the absolute. So it's the eye of the hurricane. You know, it's that calm center from which everything arises. The interesting aspect is the peace and stillness in particular are the force, the power behind all that lives, all manifestation. So it's quite impressive to make that contact. But we have to go meditatively closer to cessation. I did a retreat on cessation, and what I found, I coined this term, the cessation waiting room, is that people could get deep enough to where they could feel the draw of cessation and the magnitude of it, but they weren't quite ready to say a complete yes. They weren't ready to let go fully. And so they abide in that waiting room, getting close enough to steep and realize it's okay, it's okay, it's okay, to where at some point they may be able to say yes. transcript.text: And there's a fine point I want to ask about there when you say lights-out, because we find people talking about, I think, something that are two different kinds of cessation. transcript.speaker: Stephen Snyder

And what I'm seeing is not only does it do the function of each koan affords a mini Kensho or small awakening, or it could be large, but at least small, is that it seems to also resolve some of the emotional issues, psychological issues people have.
